Interdisciplinary AI course development for Fall 2026
Participants will use the *Living with AI* podcast to showcase and share their developments as works-in-progress.

These courses would offer an alternative conceptualization of AI literacy within the proposed AI in Practice microcredential—one grounded in theory and critical inquiry rather than skills acquisition. Students would develop the same operational and compositional fluencies as COM 188/288, but through engagement with questions about what AI *is*—materially, computationally, ecologically—rather than through isolated workflow exercises. This approach may prompt reconsideration of the 188/288/388 sequence itself, suggesting a more integrated model where critical understanding and practical fluency develop together. The collaborative, open-source development process will generate transferable resources for other faculty, and the course designs anticipate future scaling to large-enrollment asynchronous formats using AI-facilitated discussion pods.

A few kernels worth pulling into the IDT 590 framing:

**1. The tripartite definition of AI literacy:**
"Reading with large language models to interpret complex information. Writing with them to develop and articulate your professional reasoning. And critiquing them—understanding what they actually are."

That's crisper than what we have. The *critiquing* piece explicitly includes understanding what AI materially *is*—not magic, not cloud-based intelligence, but infrastructure.

**2. The material reality as ethical prerequisite:**
"AI is not magic or cloud-based intelligence. It runs on material infrastructure: data centers that consume energy, minerals extracted from the ground, labor systems. Understanding this material reality is how you use AI responsibly."

This connects the infrastructural scholarship directly to the literacy framing—it's not just academic context, it's *necessary for responsible use*.

**3. AI literacy as prerequisite for professional judgment:**
The argument that literacy isn't optional enrichment but a baseline for competent practice across fields. This strengthens the case for why this course matters.

---

**Suggested revision to the IDT 590 description (80 words):**

A collaborative course development seminar producing openly licensed curricula that prepare students to critically inhabit AI-mediated environments. AI literacy here means reading, writing, and critiquing *with* AI—understanding not just how to use these tools but what they materially are: data centers, energy consumption, labor systems.</untrusted_external_data></chat>

<chat url="https://claude.ai/chat/38faecf4-dc39-4dc0-949c-3af015c6d603" updated_at="2026-05-04T15:56:14.434827+00:00"><untrusted_external_data source="past_conversation">Title: Morrisville / Farmingdale talks: Applied AI Literacy
Morrisville / Farmingdale talks: Applied AI Literacy
<chat_summary>**Conversation overview**

Steve Zuiker is a faculty member at SUNY Polytechnic Institute working on AI literacy frameworks, with talks being developed for SUNY Morrisville (keynote), NYHIMA (breakout session), and the Manufacturing Workforce Development Forum at SUNY Farmingdale. The conversation covered two major threads: technical work on an HTML conversation artifact and substantive intellectual development of an AI literacy framework.

On the technical side, Steve corrected Claude's initial approach to rendering the Morrisville keynote conversation as HTML — the artifact requires verbatim prompt text in summary tags, not paraphrased summaries. Claude rebuilt the artifact programmatically from the source markdown file, parsing exact prompt text. Steve then requested WCAG accessibility compliance, which produced specific fixes: prompt text color changed from muted to full contrast variable, links underlined, focus-visible outlines added, small uppercase text bolded, all color variables verified for 4.5:1 contrast ratio, and dark mode ts-color variable replacing hardcoded hex. A Cowork deployment task was written for the steve-site GitHub repo targeting /artifacts/ai-literacy-applied-contexts.html.

The substantive work developed a multi-dimensional taxonomy distinguishing AI literacy contexts. The central distinction is between compositional AI users (prompt → text → revise/argue), computational users (data → analysis → interpret), and directive users (recommendation → act or don't). Steve identified that most existing AI literacy pedagogy was built for compositional contexts and is insufficient for applied/directive contexts like nursing, automotive, manufacturing, and agriculture. This led to a five-dimension framework with 756 voxels: cognitive_mode, failure_mode (perseveration, anchoring, automation_bias, deskilling, overtrust, fixation, delegation), ai_visibility (explicit/embedded/invisible), output_type (text/recommendation/analysis/action), and stakes (reversible/consequential/irreversible). A failure mode distribution chart was developed showing that perseveration, automation bias, fixation, and overtrust are most acute in directive contexts while delegation is most acute in compositional contexts — with the framing "we have been teaching AI literacy for the wrong context." A web search confirmed this framework goes beyond existing literature. Algorithm aversion was identified as a missing failure mode. The conversation also produced a draft email to a provost introducing the compositional/directive distinction, with Steve providing the final refined text. A detailed markdown file with four JSON code blocks (cuboid, high-priority voxels, single populated voxel, literature mining query) was produced for the zettelkasten. Steve clarified the project assignment: Morrisville keynote content belongs in ai-rtw, not DWIT.</untrusted_external_data></chat>
